Management
Contemporary cancer management requires a multimodal treatment approach often involving surgery,
chemotherapy, and radiation. Physicians from each discipline (surgery, medicine, and radiation oncology)
must have a working knowledge of each other’s specialty. Outcomes are optimized when representatives from
all involved disciplines meet and discuss treatment plans for patients with cancer at multidisciplinary tumor
boards. Teamwork, communication, and utilization of national standards for cancer care are essential.
Role of Surgery
Surgery is the oldest form of cancer therapy, and for many centuries, it was the only form. The introduction of
antisepsis and anesthesia permitted safer, less painful cancer operations. The current roles of surgery in the
management of cancer can be categorized as risk reducing, diagnostic, curative, or palliative. An improved
understanding of tumor biology, advances in imaging and surgical techniques, together with evidence-based
data from mature clinical trials, have all produced a shift from radical resections to less morbid procedures for
many solid tumors.
Prophylactic or risk-reduction surgery is increasingly being employed to remove tissue or organs at
increased risk for the subsequent development of cancer. For some procedures, such as mastectomy, the term
risk-reduction is preferred over prophylactic surgery; the operation significantly reduces but does not eliminate
the risk of breast cancer because some breast tissue is always left behind. The patient must be counseled
regarding this continuing risk. Other conditions where risk-reduction surgery is being utilized include total
gastrectomy in patients who have inherited a
CDH1
gene mutation, thyroidectomy in patients with multiple
endocrine neoplasia 2 (MEN-2) syndrome, and colectomy in patients with familial polyposis or ulcerative
colitis.
Surgeons are frequently asked to obtain tissue to provide a prompt and accurate diagnosis of cancer.
Following diagnosis, surgeons may perform any number of staging procedures, such as laparoscopy for gastric
and pancreatic cancers and mediastinoscopy for lung cancer.
Surgery with curative intent varies with the type of cancer but generally consists of en bloc resection of the
primary tumor. En bloc resection refers to removal of the entire tumor and any adjacent structures or organs
that are involved with the tumor in an effort to obtain tumor-free margins and minimize the risk of local
recurrence. An adequately performed en bloc resection also incorporates any previous biopsy incisions and
does not violate the primary tumor or tissue immediately adjacent to tumor. In general, more aggressive,
poorly differentiated cancers necessitate a wider margin of resection. Definitive operations for esophageal,
gastric, pancreatic, and colorectal cancer may require en bloc removal of the contiguous regional lymph nodes
(lymphadenectomy) in addition to removal of the primary tumor. In the absence of clinically positive lymph
nodes, sentinel lymph node (SLN) biopsy can be performed for breast cancer and melanoma, sparing node-
negative patients the morbidity of a lymph node dissection.
Metastasectomy, surgical therapy of metastatic disease, is appropriate treatment in select patients.
Important factors in determining the value of metastasectomy include the disease-free interval (elapsed time
from initial treatment to recurrence), the organ(s) of involvement, and the ability to render the patient tumor-
free with an acceptable morbidity and mortality. Examples where surgical resection of metastatic disease can
be effective include resection of hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer and pulmonary metastases from soft
tissue sarcoma.
Surgeons are increasingly asked to perform palliative (i.e., noncurative) operations on cancer patients to
improve quality of life. Examples of palliative operations include cytoreductive surgery to debulk tumors and
procedures to alleviate pain, control hemorrhage, relieve obstruction, repair a perforated viscus, or provide
nutritional support. Surgeons may also be asked to perform vascular access procedures to facilitate the delivery
of chemotherapy.
Chemotherapy
As antineoplastic drugs become more effective, more cancer patients are receiving chemotherapy as part of
their treatment. Chemotherapy can be delivered in primary, adjuvant, and neoadjuvant settings. Primary
chemotherapy refers to the delivery of chemotherapy alone without any additional therapies such as surgery or
radiation. Primary chemotherapy is used in hematologic malignancies such as leukemia and lymphoma.
Chemotherapy is frequently administered in an adjuvant fashion to patients who have undergone surgery with
curative intent but are at high risk for relapse, such as node-positive breast cancer. Neoadjuvant chemotherapy
is given to patients prior to surgery to “downsize” their tumor to either allow a less radical operation or obtain
clear resection margins. Chemotherapy can also be given locally or regionally to a tumor or the organ
containing the tumor to achieve much higher drug concentrations than can be delivered systemically.
Examples of regional chemotherapy include intraperitoneal chemotherapy for some GI tract and ovarian
tumors, isolated limb perfusion for extremity melanoma and sarcoma, and isolated hepatic artery infusion for
the management of hepatic metastases from colorectal cancer.
Hormonal Therapy
The growth of some cancers, such as breast and prostate cancer, is dependent on sex hormones. Therefore,
reductions in circulating hormone levels either by removal of the organs producing these hormones or by the
use of agents to block or antagonize a particular hormone can be useful in treating hormone-dependent
cancers.
In prostate cancer, hormonal interventions include orchiectomy or the administration of stilbestrol (a
synthetic estrogen), luteinizing-hormone-releasing hormone (LHRH) analogues (gonadorelins), or
antiandrogen drugs (cyproterone or flutamide). In breast cancer, interventions include oophorectomy or the
administration of tamoxifen (antiestrogen), progestogens (megestrol), LHRH (gonadorelin) antagonists, or
aromatase inhibitors.
Radiation Therapy
Radiation has been used in medicine for over a century since the discovery of x-rays by Wilhelm Roentgen in
1895. Pioneering primary research and preclinical work in the use of radioactive isotopes was performed by
Nobel Prize winner Marie Curie in 1898. Ever since these pioneering efforts were made, ionizing radiation
(both from external sources, called “teletherapy,” and implanted sources, called “brachytherapy”) is now
extensively used as one component of multidisciplinary cancer care. Radiation is typically delivered in multiple
doses (1 to 44) or “fractions” and may be used as the primary treatment of radiosensitive tumors, such as
seminoma and localized Hodgkin’s disease. Radiation therapy is usually used as an adjuvant to other cancer
therapies. Some chemotherapeutic agents, such as cisplatin and 5-fluorouracil, can serve as radio-sensitizers.
In some instances, radiation therapy is preferred over surgery as a cancer treatment when organ or tissue
preservation is desired, such as in laryngeal cancer, oropharyngeal cancer (particularly that which is HPV+),
and basal cell carcinoma of the face. In other clinical situations, such as lumpectomy to treat breast cancer,
adjuvant external-beam radiation is utilized after surgery to reduce the risk of local recurrence. There is
growing evidence that in the modern era, reductions in local recurrence risk may also increase disease-specific
and overall survival.
Radiotherapy may be delivered using several techniques, including teletherapy and brachytherapy as noted
earlier, or even with systemic radioisotope therapy. External-beam radiotherapy is delivered with an external
source and is the most commonly used form of radiation for the treatment of cancer worldwide. The most
typical radiation source is the linear accelerator (LINAC), which uses relativistic electrons and high-density
material to produce megavoltage-level photons. In contrast, brachytherapy is delivered with the radiation
sources near or within the target tissue. Brachytherapy is used to treat cervical, breast, prostate, and other
cancers and may be combined with external-beam radiation therapy, depending on the clinical situation.
Advances in imaging techniques have improved the targeting of radiation such that tumors can be treated
with less toxicity to surrounding normal tissues. Iodine
, a radioisotope, is used for the systemic treatment of
thyroid cancer and has historically been the most common systemic radioisotope used in the clinical setting.
Stereotactic radiation is a specialized, highly focused type of external-beam radiation therapy in which the
tumor is precisely targeted using detailed imaging scans combined with motion management (of both the
patient and the tumor itself). Stereotactic radiation has historically been used to treat only brain and spinal
cord tumors; however, recent advances in both technique and evidence have brought stereotactic radiation to
the forefront of management in various organ systems.
The molecular mechanism of radiotherapy involves both direct and indirect action upon the DNA with
resultant changes injurious to the genetic framework that promotes either apoptotic or karyorrhexis cascades.
Typically, the bulk of the DNA damage results from indirect actions, wherein free radical particles produced
by ionizing radiation cause irreparable DNA damage. Direct action is more typical of very high-energy
therapeutic photons or other types of charged particle teletherapy and causes DNA strand breaks without a
free radical intermediary. Although both cancer cells and normal cells are affected, most of the normal cells
recover and continue to function. Complications of radiation therapy include lethargy, skin rashes,
desquamation, nausea, vomiting, anorexia, urinary frequency, mouth dryness, impaired blood supply, and
delayed healing.
Photodynamic Therapy
Photodynamic therapy (PDT) is a cancer treatment that uses a photosensitizer drug and a light source to
promote free radical formation to destroy sensitized cells. The singlet oxygen that is created destroys cells
directly or by destroying nearby blood vessels and may activate the immune system to attack the affected
tumor cells. PDT is currently used to relieve the symptoms of esophageal cancer and non–small cell lung
cancer and to treat precancerous mucosal lesions in Barrett’s esophagus. It is also used to treat nonmelanotic
skin cancers and premalignant skin lesions such as actinic keratosis.
Targeted, Biologic, and Evolving Cancer Therapies
Tremendous progress has been made in our basic understanding of cancer, and research advances continue to
translate into improvements in cancer management. Targeted therapy uses drugs or other agents that block
the growth and spread of cancer by interfering with specific molecules involved in tumor growth. Such agents
can inhibit growth factor receptors, intracellular signal transduction, or the cell cycle. The most widely used is
a monoclonal antibody, Herceptin (trastuzumab), which targets the overexpressed HER-2 growth factor
receptor on some breast cancer cells.
Cancer immunotherapy uses substances to either activate or inhibit the patient’s own immune system to
fight cancer. Immunotherapy may be active or passive, specific or nonspecific. Bacillus Calmette-Guerin is an
active nonspecific stimulant of the immune system used for superficial bladder cancer, whereas specific active
immunotherapy includes vaccines derived from tumor cells or antigen-presenting cells. Passive
immunotherapy is conferred by cytokines, such as interferon (INF), which enhance a patient’s antitumor
response by activating white blood cells such as natural killer cells and dendritic cells. INF-
α
is utilized as
immunotherapy in the treatment of melanoma, Kaposi sarcoma, and several hematologic cancers.
Gene therapy attempts to alter the genetic program of cancer cells by introducing DNA or RNA into
living cells. Many strategies are under investigation, including replacing an altered tumor suppressor gene such
as
TP53
or introducing genetic material to block tumor oncogene expression.
Prevention
Cancer prevention can be primary (in otherwise healthy persons), secondary (in those who have premalignant
conditions), or tertiary (avoiding second malignancies in those cured of their original disease). National
organizations such as the American Cancer Society have established recommendations for lifestyle changes
that reduce an individual’s risk of developing cancer. Research in chemoprevention in high-risk individuals is
ongoing and current options include tamoxifen to prevent breast cancer, nicotinamide (vitamin B
) for the
prevention of nonmelanotic skin cancers, and 13-cis-retinoic acid to reverse leukoplakia. Prevention can also
be achieved surgically for those patients found to be at increased risk genetically or once found to harbor
premalignant lesions, as discussed earlier. Guidelines for the long-term follow-up of patients with cancer are
outlined in the NCCN guidelines.
MALIGNANT DISEASES OF THE SKIN
The skin is the largest organ in the human body, and skin cancer is the most common malignant tumor.
There are over 1 million new cases of skin cancer annually in the United States, accounting for approximately
35% to 40% of all new cancers. Cutaneous malignancies are typically divided into two broad categories:
melanoma and nonmelanoma skin cancers. Most skin cancers arise in the outermost layer of the skin, the
epidermis, and consequently they are visible at an early, highly curable stage. Therefore, all physicians must
recognize the early signs and symptoms of skin cancer, and they should also be familiar with the preferred
diagnostic methods.
Basal Cell and Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Convincing evidence exists that ultraviolet (UV) radiation causes skin cancer. Skin cancer is more common in
fair-skinned, sun-sensitive individuals and on sun-exposed parts of the body. The incidence of skin cancer is
also higher as solar radiation increases at higher elevations and decreasing latitudes. In addition, those
individuals who are subject to occupational (e.g., farmers or fishermen) or recreational (e.g., sun-bathers) sun
exposure have a higher incidence of skin cancer.
UV light is electromagnetic radiation with a wavelength in the range 290 to 400 nm. Sunlight consists of
two main types of UV radiation, UVA and UVB, both of which contribute to freckling, skin wrinkling, and
the development of skin cancer. UVB radiation (290 to 320 nm) has more energy than UVA radiation and it
causes the most skin damage. UVA radiation (320 to 400 nm) is the light used in tanning booths and is less
powerful than UVB; however, UVA penetrates deeper into the skin. The cumulative effect of solar radiation
causes irreversible skin damage, and overexposure to UV radiation may cause skin cancer via direct or indirect
damage to DNA with point mutations in the p53 tumor suppressor gene. Skin cancers are often seen in
association with other solar radiation–induced skin damage, including wrinkling, telangiectasias (dilated blood
vessels), actinic keratosis (erythematous, rough-surfaced lesions), and solar elastosis (yellow papules). Because
exposure to the sun is modifiable behavior, there is an opportunity for the primary prevention of skin cancer
by educating patients about the hazards of sun exposure and tanning beds and their contribution to increasing
rates of skin cancers.
Basal cell carcinoma (BCC) and squamous cell carcinoma (SCC) account for about 70% and 25%,
respectively, of nonmelanoma skin cancers. The incidence of nonmelanoma skin cancer increases with age,
with most patients being older than 65 years of age at the time of diagnosis, which is likely due to lifetime
cumulative exposure to UV radiation. There is a 3:1 predominance of these tumors in men, attributed partially
to greater outdoor employment. Fortunately, the cure rate for nonmelanoma skin cancers is high when they
are recognized and biopsied early. Delayed diagnosis of skin cancer requires wider resections, with complex
reconstructions producing greater cosmetic and functional deformities (Figures 22-1 and 22-2). Furthermore,
although BCCs rarely metastasize, large, poorly differentiated SCCs can spread locally, regionally, and
distantly. SCCs most commonly spread to the regional lymphatic basin and less commonly to distant sites
such as the lungs and liver. Despite early detection efforts, approximately 2,000 individuals die from
nonmelanoma skin cancers annually.

Prolonged chemical exposure is also implicated in the development of skin cancer. Sir Percivall Pott, an
English surgeon, demonstrated the relationship between exposure to soot and carcinoma of the skin of the
scrotum in chimney sweeps. Other examples include arsenic, paraffin oil, creosote, pitch, fuel oil, coal, and
psoralens with UVA photochemotherapy. Cigarette smoking is also associated with SCC of the lip, mouth,
and nonmucosal skin.
Skin cancer can also arise in areas of chronic inflammation such as burns, scars, ulcers, and sinus tracts
(e.g. at the site of a chronic osteomyelitis infection, chronic pilonidal sinus, hidradenitis suppurativa). SCC
arising in a chronic nonhealing wound is referred to as a Marjolin’s ulcer. Skin cancers that develop in chronic
wounds are aggressive and have an increased risk of local recurrence, distant spread, and poor outcome. Any
chronic wound that fails to heal or undergoes a recent change should be biopsied (Figure 22-3).
Viral infections also play a role in the development of some skin cancers. HPV is the virus that can cause
condyloma acuminata or genital warts. In 1925, Buschke and Löwenstein first described a large, cauliflower-
like, verrucous cancer that develops in a giant condyloma acuminata (Figure 22-4). HPV type 6 or 11 is
regularly found in association with this aggressive tumor. Risk factors for these tumors include
immunosuppression, chronic irritation, and poor personal hygiene in the anogenital area. Large cauliflower-
like genital warts should be biopsied in multiple areas to determine whether SCC is present. Patients with
giant condyloma acuminata and multiple fistulous tracts, purulent discharge, or involvement of the anal
sphincter may require a colostomy to prevent fecal soilage. The definitive treatment for giant condyloma
acuminata is radical surgical excision often requiring tissue flap reconstruction, but despite radical surgery,
there is still a high rate of local failure.
Genetic and ethnic factors play an important predisposing role in the development of SCC and BCC.
Caucasians with light hair and blue eyes are at greater risk than those populations with darker skin
pigmentation. The increased melanin in ethnic groups with darker skin pigmentation may afford protection
against the damage caused by solar radiation. Chronically immunosuppressed individuals, such as patients
who have undergone solid organ transplantation, have HIV, or who are long-term steroid users are at
increased risk for more aggressive cancers. Therefore, sun-protective measures are extremely important in this
high-risk group of patients.
Although less commonly used today for benign conditions, therapeutic radiation is another physical agent
that is responsible for the development of malignant skin tumors, usually SCC. This phenomenon is
particularly true for dentists and physicians who used x-ray equipment without appropriate protection and in
patients who received radiation treatment for benign skin conditions such as acne.
Basal Cell Carcinoma
Clinical and Histopathologic Characteristics
BCC arises from the basal layer of the epidermis and its appendages such as hair follicles and sebaceous
glands. These cancers typically grow slowly and almost never metastasize. Untreated, they can produce
considerable morbidity through local invasion and destruction of surrounding normal tissue. These cancers
spread microscopically a significant distance beyond the grossly visible tumor. Histologically, BCC consists of
masses of darkly stained tumor cells that grow from the basal layer of epithelium into the dermis and
subcutaneous tissue. BCC causes no pain or discomfort, and the patient may defer seeking medical attention
until the lesion is well advanced. Alternatively, the patient may first seek care because of troublesome bleeding
from the tumor when it is traumatized, such as by shaving. Approximately 70% of BCCs occur on the face
secondary to sun exposure. The clinical presentation of BCC is divided into three main groups: nodular,
superficial, and morpheaform.
Nodular BCC is the most common type and generally appears on the face as a smooth, dome-shaped,
round, waxy, or pearly papule (Figure 22-5). Nodular BCC is slow growing and it may take as long as 1 year
to double in size. Nodular BCC may have telangiectasias or small dilated blood vessels on the surface that
bleed when traumatized. As the tumor outgrows its blood supply, the center of the lesion undergoes necrosis,
forming an ulcer with the potential to invade deeply into adjacent structures (rodent ulcer). Pigmented BCC
contains melanocytes that give it a dark brown or a blue-black color and may be confused with melanoma.
Approximately 30% of BCCs are the superficial subtype, and they occur more frequently on the trunk.
Superficial BCCs frequently present as a shiny, scaly papule, or erythematous patch that may be atrophic in
the center. These tumors may also appear multicentric with areas of normal-appearing skin between areas of
involved skin.
Morpheaform or sclerosing BCC accounts for approximately 5% to 10% of BCC. It typically appears as a
smooth, indurated, yellow plaque with ill-defined borders. The overlying skin may remain intact, leading to a
delay in diagnosis. The skin looks shiny and taut because the tumor causes an intense fibroblastic response
that gives it a scar-like appearance. The true margin of this form of BCC is difficult to determine because the
tumor cells invade normal tissue well beyond the visible margins. Therefore, sclerosing BCC should be treated
with a wide excision with careful attention to the margins.
Treatment
Excision is the preferred management for BCC. The surgical goal is complete removal of the tumor with
minimal functional deformity and optimal cosmetic outcome. The NCCN guidelines recommend a 4-mm
margin for low-risk tumors (size <2 cm, well-defined borders, no immunosuppression, no prior radiation
therapy, nodular or superficial subtypes, and no perineural invasion). A wider margin is recommended for
high-risk BCCs. Cryotherapy (freezing the tumor) or electrodessication and curettage (using a sharp spoon-
like instrument or curette with electrocautery) can be used to treat small BCCs (≤0.5 cm), but no histology or
margin status is then available. Both methods are fast and cost-effective and can be performed in an office
setting with local anesthesia. Both treatments take several weeks to heal and may result in hypopigmentation
and scarring. Moh’s micrographic surgical technique may be used to remove BCCs that arise or recur in
cosmetically sensitive areas, such as the face, where there is a need to preserve normal tissue and cosmesis.
This technique consists of carefully labeling and orienting the specimens at the time of excision (e.g., superior
margin, anterior) and creating a diagram (Moh’s map) of the position of the specimen in relation to the
surrounding structures. A pathologist then carefully examines frozen sections to determine proximity of the
tumor to the resection margin. Additional tissue is sent for frozen-section examination until tumor-free
margins are achieved. When the margins are determined to be clear of tumor, the surgical wound is either
closed primarily, skin-grafted, covered with a tissue flap, or dressed in anticipation of secondary definitive
wound coverage. This careful, stepwise excision with immediate pathologic assessment of margins ensures
that all margins are free of residual tumor and preserves normal skin.
Topical chemotherapy using 5-fluorouracil (5-FU, Efudex) cream can be useful in patients with too many
superficial BCCs to excise or in patients with extensive skin damage. The treatment requires application of a
lotion or cream once or twice per day for approximately 1 month. The dosage is adjusted (1%, 2%, or 5% 5-
FU concentration) to achieve moderate erythema. The inflammatory reaction and erythema causes some
patients to discontinue treatment.
Finally, radiation therapy is a treatment option for elderly patients with BCC who are not surgical
candidates. As with other ablative therapies, primary radiation therapy permits no histologic assessment of the
tumor or margins.
Prognosis
Surgical excision cures most patients with BCC; however, incomplete excision can result in recurrence at the
site of tumor removal. Approximately 20% of patients who have a single BCC develop a new primary lesion
within 1 year, whereas patients with multiple tumors have a 40% risk of developing a second BCC within 1
year. Therefore, long-term skin surveillance at 6-month to 1-year intervals is imperative after tumor resection
in all patients with BCC. These patients must also be educated about the hazards of UV radiation and the
importance of sun-safe behaviors.
Squamous Cell Carcinoma
Clinical and Histopathologic Characteristics
SCC arises from the keratinocytes of the epidermis. Unlike BCC, SCC has the potential for metastatic
spread, and the risk of metastasis of SCC correlates with size and the grade (i.e., percentage of
undifferentiated cells) of the lesion. The most common site of metastasis for SCC is the regional lymph
nodes, whereas distant sites include the lung, liver, and brain. SCC most commonly presents as an ulcerated,
erythematous nodule or erosion with indistinct borders (Figure 22-6). It is most commonly found on the
lower lip and elsewhere in the head and neck as well as in other areas of sun-damaged skin. The tumor may
arise
de novo
or from an area with preexisting skin damage, burn scars, chronic ulcers, osteomyelitic sinuses, or
chronic granulomas. Multiple biopsies should be performed on any chronic nonhealing ulcer that is increasing
in size and is not responding to appropriate therapy. SCC
in situ,
or Bowen’s disease, is characterized by
tumor cells that have not yet broken through the epidermal–dermal junction. Bowen’s disease clinically
resembles a red patch or crusting plaque and without treatment can progress to invasive SCC. The overall rate
of metastasis for SCC is low (approximately 1%–2%). However, tumors that arise in burns, draining
osteomyelitic sinuses, chronic ulcers, and Bowen’s disease tend to metastasize more often than tumors that
arise in sun-damaged skin.
Figure 22-6
Squamous cell carcinoma of the arm with a nodular appearance and central ulceration.
Most SCCs appear clinically as an erythematous firm papule on normal or sun-damaged skin. SCC may
initially be difficult to distinguish from a hyperkeratotic lesion, but as the tumor enlarges, it forms a nodule
with central ulceration and a white or yellow necrotic base. Typically, SCC does not have the pearly, raised
margins of BCC. SCCs often have crusts or scabs because of repetitive trauma and bleeding. As with BCC
lesions, SCC lesions may enlarge and destroy adjacent normal tissue.
Microscopically, the tumors are irregular nests of epidermal cells that infiltrate the dermis to varying
depths and show varying degrees of differentiation. The more differentiated the tumor is, the greater is the
number of epithelial pearls (keratinous material) seen in the depths of the tumor.
Treatment
Surgical excision is the preferred treatment for SCC. The recommended margin of resection is 4 to 6 mm,
and the same criteria apply for closure of the defect resulting from excision of SCC as with BCC. However,
because SCC has the potential to spread via lymphatics, regional lymph node basins need to be assessed. In
patients with nonpalpable nodes, a sentinel node biopsy is an option for patients with high-risk lesions such as
those that are larger than 2.0 cm in diameter, are poorly differentiated, demonstrate perineural invasion, or are
2 mm or more in thickness. In patients who have palpable or image-detected nodal disease, a fine-needle
aspiration (FNA) or core biopsy is performed. Patients with histologically proven lymph node metastases
require lymph node dissection. Per NCCN guidelines, patients at high risk for local and regional recurrence
may also benefit from adjuvant radiation therapy to the excision site and regional lymph node basins.
In addition to cryotherapy, electrodessication, and topical 5-FU, other nonsurgical treatments for SCC
in
situ
include photodynamic therapy and the topical immune response modifier imiquimod. PDT uses
porphyrins to produce tumor cell cytotoxicity after stimulation by light of a certain wavelength. Imiquimod
takes advantage of the antitumor properties of immune cells and local cytokine production. Nonsurgical
therapies do not allow histologic analysis of margins and may require a high number of treatments to ensure
complete removal of the lesion.
Prognosis
The prognosis for small SCCs is excellent, with a cure rate of 95%. In larger lesions that penetrate the
subcutaneous tissue, however, the risk of nodal metastasis increases substantially and after lymph node
involvement occurs, prognosis is poor. Two-thirds of patients with SCC that has penetrated into the
subcutaneous tissue may ultimately die from metastatic disease. Thus, rigorous follow-up is recommended,
which includes an examination every 6 months for local recurrence, evidence of regional nodal metastasis, or
new lesions.
Merkel Cell Carcinoma
Merkel cell carcinoma (MCC) is a tumor that is becoming more prevalent. MCC tends to manifest in
Caucasians from 60 to 80 years of age and usually arises as a small, firm, painless nodule that varies in size
from 0.5 to 5 cm. More than half arise in the sun-exposed areas of the body, but about 12% may be metastatic
without a known primary site. The major cause is the Merkel cell polyomavirus, which is integrated into a
monoclonal pattern. The diagnosis should be suspected with the clinical presentation, and confirmatory
biopsy should be performed. MCCs are aggressive, spreading hematogenously to the liver, brain, lungs, and
bone, and any MCC greater than 1 cm in diameter should undergo SLN biopsy as well. Negative surgical
margins should be the goal. Because MCCs are aggressive tumors, adjuvant radiation therapy reduces the
rates for recurrence and increases survival. A newer chemotherapeutic agent, avelumab, may be beneficial as
well.
Melanoma
Incidence and Etiology
The incidence of melanoma is increasing at an exponential rate (Figure 22-7). Over the last half of the
twentieth century, diagnosis of melanoma has increased over 600%, whereas the death rate has risen over
160%. Although this increase in incidence may, in part, be the result of an increasing number of skin biopsies
performed, it does not appear to be the result of more complete reporting or an alteration in the pathologic
criteria for the diagnosis of melanoma. In fact, the incidence of melanoma may even be higher than the
aforementioned rate because some melanomas are treated by destructive methods. Furthermore, many
hospital-based tumor registries do not capture patients with melanoma diagnosed and treated elsewhere.
Figure 22-7
Graph illustrating the exponential increase in the lifetime risk of melanoma.
Although melanoma accounts only for 4% of cutaneous malignancies, it accounts for 80% of all deaths
from skin cancer. There are an estimated 60,000 new cases of melanoma and 8,000 deaths from melanoma
yearly in the United States. Currently, melanoma is the fifth most common cancer in men and the seventh
most common in women, but it is the most common cancer in women of ages 20 to 29. The incidence of
melanoma increases with age from 0.4 cases per 100,000 people aged 10 to 19 years to 35 cases per 100,000
people older than 80 years. In addition, the lifetime risk of developing melanoma is currently estimated to be
UV radiation, usually from sunlight, is the primary cause of melanoma. The pattern, timing, and duration
of exposure to UV radiation are all important in melanoma development. For example, melanoma caused by
intense episodic exposure to sunlight in areas that are infrequently exposed to sunlight, such as the back, is a
common occurrence. However, melanomas occur with increased incidence on the legs in women and on the
trunk in men. These data suggest that exposure to sunlight has a role in the etiology of melanoma, but they do
not account for the occurrence of melanoma in areas of the body that have minimal exposure to sunlight.
Location of exposure is also important, with several studies in Australia, New Zealand, and the United
States showing an increased incidence of melanoma near the equator.
Sunburn is a marker of excessive episodic exposure to UV radiation and, if occurring in childhood and
adolescence, appears to do the most damage, leading to a subsequent development of melanoma. Therefore,
efforts to educate the public about the hazards of UV radiation and the importance of sun-safe behaviors
should begin in childhood. The American Cancer Society recommends prime time sun avoidance, sun-
protective clothing, frequent reapplication of broad-spectrum sunblock with >30 SPF, and avoidance of
tanning beds. The incidence of melanoma is influenced by skin pigment, with the lowest rates (0.8 per
100,000 population) occurring among blacks. On the contrary, incidence rates among the Celtic population in
Australia and New Zealand are the highest in the world (40 per 100,000). The so-called melanoma phenotype
consists of fair-complexioned individuals with blue eyes and red or blonde hair who freckle and burn easily
upon brief sun exposure.
The location of melanomas is variable, with approximately one-fourth of all cutaneous melanomas
occurring in the head and neck area. Of these, the majority occurs outside the hair-bearing scalp. However,
the site distribution of malignant melanoma in blacks is strikingly different from that in whites, with
approximately 70% of melanomas found on the palmar surface of the hands and plantar surface of the feet of
blacks, compared with <5% in whites. Approximately 50% to 60% of melanomas arise from or near benign
nevi. Benign nevi are extremely common and very few become malignant, and the triggering event for
malignant transformation of benign nevi remains unknown. The one exception is congenital giant hairy nevus
(bathing trunk nevus), which undergoes malignant transformation to melanoma in 10% to 30% of untreated
lesions.
Familial malignant melanomas account for approximately 10% of all melanomas, but almost half of
patients who have multiple primary melanomas have a family history of melanoma. Familial melanomas tend
to occur at a younger age than sporadic tumors. In addition, any patient who has experienced a melanoma is at
risk for a second melanoma.
A third recognized risk factor for hereditary melanoma is familial atypical mole and melanoma syndrome
(FAM-M), previously called dysplastic nevus syndrome. Patients with familial melanoma have large
premalignant nevi, predominantly over the shoulders, upper chest, and back. Hereditary melanoma and
FAM-M are associated with genetic alterations in chromosomes 1p, 6q, 7, and 9; the genetic predisposition
to malignant melanoma is also associated with the hereditary syndrome xeroderma pigmentosum, which is an
autosomal recessive disorder characterized by defective DNA repair mechanisms required to repair damage
caused by UV radiation.
Clinical and Histopathologic Characteristics
Melanoma is classified into four main morphologic subtypes: superficial spreading melanoma, nodular
melanoma, lentigo maligna melanoma, and acral lentiginous melanoma. The T stage of tumor thickness, and
ulceration, is predictive of outcome rather than the subtype. Melanoma has two distinct growth patterns:
horizontal and vertical. The horizontal, or lateral, growth phase results in increasing lesion diameter but not
an increased risk of distant spread. The vertical growth phase increases the likelihood of invasion, access to the
lymphatics and/or blood vessels, and potential for metastatic spread.
Superficial spreading melanoma is the most common subtype of melanoma, accounting for approximately
70% of all cutaneous melanomas. It is most commonly found on the legs in women and on the back in men.
The peak incidence of superficial spreading melanoma occurs in the fifth decade. This tumor has both radial
and vertical growth phases. Early superficial spreading melanoma lesions are of many colors (usually tan,
brown, blue, and black). More advanced lesions have palpable nodularity, indicating the development of a
vertical growth phase. Some of these tumors have depigmented areas representing spontaneous regression
(Figure 22-8).
Figure 22-8
Superficial spreading melanoma demonstrating areas of regression.
Nodular melanoma accounts for approximately 10% to 15% of all cutaneous melanomas and is the most
malignant subtype because of a dominant vertical growth phase. Nodular melanoma occurs twice as often in
men as in women (Figure 22-9). The host cellular response is usually less than that seen with other types of
melanoma. Nodular melanoma is blue-black in color with less variability in color and margins than superficial
spreading melanoma.
Figure 22-9
Nodular melanoma.
Lentigo maligna melanoma (Hutchinson’s freckle) is the least aggressive subtype of melanoma and is
characterized by slow, insidious growth. It tends to occur on the sun-exposed areas of the face, head, and neck
of older people. This type of melanoma constitutes 5% to 10% of cutaneous melanomas. It usually begins as a
circumscribed macular patch of mottled pigmentation, showing shades of dark brown, tan, or black (Figure
22-10). It is often referred to as “a stain on the skin.” The median age at diagnosis is approximately 70 years,
and women are affected more often than men. Although lentigo maligna melanoma has a slow, benign-
appearing growth pattern, the margins are ill-defined, and therefore achieving a tumor-free margin can be
challenging.

Acral lentiginous melanoma occurs on the palmar surface of the hands and the plantar surface of the feet
(Figure 22-11) and in subungual (i.e., beneath the nail plate) sites (Figure 22-12). Acral lentiginous
melanoma has both radial and vertical growth phases. Clinically, in the subungual location, the radial growth
phase may be a streak in the nail associated with irregular tan-brown staining of the nail bed. Subungual
melanomas frequently distort the nail plate and are often misdiagnosed as a fungal infection, resulting in a
delay in diagnosis.

Diagnosis
Because the skin is accessible to direct visual inspection, cutaneous melanoma is amenable to early detection
and diagnosis. Patients with early stage “thin” melanomas (thickness < 1.0 mm) have a 5-year survival rate of
90%. A complete skin exam in a well-lit room is an essential part of any physical examination. A magnifying
glass can be of value, and the clinician must inspect the scalp, palms, soles, and mucosa. A convenient
mnemonic for the recognition of melanoma is the ABCDE rule:
Any lesions exhibiting the above-mentioned criteria should be biopsied. Lesions that are occasionally
confused with cutaneous melanoma include junctional nevi, compound nevi, intradermal nevi, blue nevi,
BCCs, seborrheic keratoses, dermatofibromas, and subungual hemorrhage.
Full-thickness excisional biopsy down to subcutaneous tissue with a 1-to 3-mm margin of normal-
appearing skin is the preferred method of biopsy. Excisional biopsy permits histopathologic analysis of the
entire lesion to determine the depth of penetration. Accurate staging is critical for the management of
melanoma. On the extremities, the incision is placed parallel to the long axis to facilitate primary closure. If
the size or location of the primary site prevents excisional biopsy, then an incisional or punch biopsy is
performed.
However, the possibility of sampling error must be considered when incisional or punch biopsy is
performed. Shave biopsy is
not
the preferred method of biopsy because it fails to provide an accurate depth of
invasion. In addition, shave biopsy can result in inflammatory cells at the base of the lesion that make a precise
determination of the depth of invasion difficult when definitive excision follows a shave biopsy.
Staging
The characteristics of melanoma that are important in determining subsequent management and prognosis are
tumor thickness, ulceration, nodal metastases, and distant metastases. Two systems are used to determine the
depth of invasion, which predicts the risk of metastasis and determines the margin width required for re-
excision. The Breslow system utilizes thickness of the tumor in millimeters from the granular layer of the
epidermis to the deepest point of vertical growth. The Breslow system allows objective evaluation and easier
comparison among pathologists. The Clark system for staging primary melanoma is based on the histologic
level of invasion of the tumor. Level 1, or melanoma
in situ
, involves melanoma confined to the epidermis,
level 2 involves invasion into papillary dermis, level 3 involves invasion to the junction of the papillary and
reticular dermis, level 4 involves invasion into the reticular dermis, and level 5 involves deep invasion into the
subcutaneous fat. A disadvantage of the Clark system is that pathologists may differ in their interpretation of
the level of invasion. In addition, the Clark level is used only for staging when the Breslow tumor thickness is
The AJCC TNM system uses information from the Breslow system, considers whether the lesion is
ulcerated, and adds information about the status of lymph nodes and distant metastases to provide a
comprehensive staging system. (See also https://www.cancer.org/cancer/melanoma-skin-cancer/detection-
diagnosis-staging/melanoma-skin-cancer-stages.html.)
Malignant melanoma can spread through both lymphatic and hematogenous routes. Lymphatic spread
can present clinically as in-transit metastases or as enlarged regional nodes. In-transit metastases occur when
melanoma cells are trapped between the primary tumor and regional lymph nodes and produce a region of
subcutaneous metastases more than 3 cm from the primary site. Distant metastasis from melanoma occurs
most commonly in skin, subcutaneous tissue, and distant lymph nodes. Lung, brain, liver, and bone are less
frequent sites and convey a worse prognosis.
Treatment
Definitive surgical treatment of primary melanoma involves a wide excision of the surrounding normal skin
and subcutaneous tissue. The goal of wide local excision is to remove all melanoma cells while minimizing
morbidity, cosmetic disfigurement, functional impairment, and cost. The recommended width of excision of a
melanoma has declined over the last 20 to 30 years, and there are now evidence-based guidelines for margins
of excision dependent on the tumor thickness. A margin of 1.0 cm is generally recommended for thin
melanomas ≤1.0 mm in depth. For melanomas >1 mm thick, 2-cm margins of excision are recommended.
Most wide excisions can be closed primarily and skin grafts avoided.
If regional lymph nodes are palpable on physical examination, regional node dissection is performed. In
the absence of lymphadenopathy, SLN biopsy can accurately stage patients by determining the histologic
status of the draining nodes. Per NCCN guidelines, SLN biopsy should be discussed with patients whose
melanomas are <0.8 mm combined with adverse features, or ≥0.8 mm. Adverse features include high mitotic
age in a young patient or lymphovascular invasion. SLNs are the principal nodes that drain the skin where the
melanoma is located and provide prognostic information about the remainder of the lymph node basin. The
technique of SLN biopsy involves the use of a dye and/or a radiolabeled material injected intradermally
around the primary site of the melanoma. An incision is made over the draining regional lymph basin, and all
clinically suspicious, radioactive, and/or blue lymph nodes are removed. If the sentinel nodes are negative,
there is a >95% chance that the remaining lymph nodes are tumor free. If the sentinel node is positive, then a
complete node dissection is recommended for staging and local control. The sensitivity and predictive value of
SLN biopsy can be improved using immunohistochemistry methods that identify proteins unique to
melanoma cells and using reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction to identify genes unique to
melanoma cells. Although these methods increase the sensitivity of melanoma detection, the routine use of
reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction in staging melanoma is still under evaluation to determine its
utility and predictive value.
Adjuvant treatment is given in addition to primary surgical therapy when all detectable disease has been
removed, but where there remains a high risk of relapse because of occult disease. Patients with melanoma
should be managed in a multidisciplinary setting and patients with advanced disease should be offered clinical
trial enrollment. For stages IIB and IIC, IFN-
α
, a proinflammatory cytokine, can be given. For stage III
melanoma, with involved regional lymph nodes, options also include immunotherapy such as nivolumab,
ipilimumab, and agents that target mutated
BRAF
genes. Local recurrences and in-transit metastases can be
treated with intralesional injection or isolated limb perfusion with chemotherapeutic agents.
Most distant metastases develop within 5 years of diagnosis, but delayed recurrences of melanoma may
occur even decades after diagnosis. Surgery is the main treatment for metastatic melanoma. Although
resection of isolated distant metastasis may improve survival and quality of life, it is rarely curative. Metastatic
disease to the brain can be treated with stereotactic radiosurgery or resection followed by adjuvant
radiotherapy (RT). Pulmonary and liver metastases may be resected depending upon the disease-free interval,
location, and the number of metastases. Hepatic metastases may be ablated by nonresectional methods such as
radiofrequency ablation. Cytotoxic chemotherapy regimens and adjuvant RT can also be considered for
metastatic and unresectable disease.
Like other skin cancers, melanoma requires close follow-up with yearly skin exams for life. Full-body skin
examinations should occur every 6 to 12 months for the first 5 years, and annually thereafter. During these
examinations, any signs or symptoms of metastatic disease should be investigated using radiographic imaging.
MALIGNANT DISEASES OF THE SOFT TISSUE
Sarcoma
Adult soft tissue sarcomas (STS) are rare tumors derived from embryonic mesoderm that represent
approximately 1% of adult malignancies. STS can develop from fat, muscle, nerves, blood vessels, and other
connective tissues. The evaluation and treatment of patients with STS require a multidisciplinary team with
demonstrated expertise in the management of these tumors.
There are over 100 subtypes of STS in the most recent WHO classification, the most common being
undifferentiated high-grade pleomorphic sarcoma, gastrointestinal stromal tumor (GIST), liposarcoma,
leiomyosarcoma, synovial sarcoma, and malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumors. Although ectodermal in
origin, peripheral nerve sheath tumors are included in this group because of similarities in behavior and
management with STS. The location of the primary tumor strongly influences treatment and outcome. The
approximate anatomic distribution is as follows: leg, 40%; trunk, 15.5%; pelvis, 15%; arm, 14%; abdomen, 8%;
and head and neck, 7%. Tumor stage is strongly influenced by the grade of the tumor, taking into
consideration cellular differentiation, mitotic count, and tumor necrosis. STS rarely metastasize to regional
lymph nodes, more commonly spreading to the lungs or to the peritoneum and liver in the case of abdominal
tumors.
Incidence and Etiology
There are approximately 13,000 new cases and 5,000 deaths from sarcoma annually in the United States. It is
thought that sarcomas arrive
de novo
and not from a preexisting benign lesion. For the majority of patients,
the etiology is unknown. Patients with sarcoma may present with a history of trauma that calls attention to
the area; however, a causal relationship has never been established. Risk factors that have been associated with
sarcoma occurrence include occupational exposures, radiation, chronic lymphedema, viral infections, and both
germline and somatic mutations in oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes.
A variety of chemical agents and carcinogens have been linked to the development of sarcoma. Asbestos
(hydrated silicate) is associated with the development of pleural mesothelioma. Exposure to phenoxyacetic
acid herbicides (lawn pesticides) and their by-products has been associated with increased incidence of
sarcomas. Exposure to arsenic and polyvinyl chloride has been associated with the development of the
particularly aggressive hepatic angiosarcoma.
There is an 8-to 50-fold increase in incidence of sarcoma reported in patients treated with high-dose
radiation for carcinoma of the breast, cervix, ovary, testes, and lymphatic system. To be diagnosed as a
radiation-associated sarcoma, the lesion must be in the radiated field, be of a different histology than the
primary irradiated tumor, and develop after a latency period of at least 3 years. The most common type of
STS seen in irradiated fields is undifferentiated pleomorphic sarcoma, previously known as malignant fibrous
histiocytoma. Postirradiation cutaneous angiosarcoma can arise in irradiated tissues at a shorter time interval
than other STS. Angiosarcoma can also arise in the context of arm lymphedema after axillary dissection for a
carcinoma of the breast, which is known as Stewart-Treves syndrome.
Germline mutations in the tumor suppressor gene p53 cause the Li-Fraumeni syndrome and increase the
risk of rhabdomyosarcoma, osteosarcoma, and other STSs, as well as brain tumors, early-onset breast
carcinoma, leukemia, and adrenocortical carcinoma. Germline mutations in the neurofibromatosis type l gene
NF1
produce Von Recklinghausen syndrome with an associated 10% lifetime risk of malignant peripheral
nerve sheath tumors (MPNST, or neurofibrosarcoma). Gardner’s syndrome (a subset of familial polyposis
patients) is associated with an increased incidence of desmoid tumors (aggressive fibromatosis). The familial
polyposis syndromes are caused by a mutation in the adenomatous polyposis coli (
APC
) gene. Patients with
familial or bilateral types of inherited retinoblastoma carry a mutant copy of the
RB
gene and are predisposed
to secondary bone and soft tissue tumors.
A high percentage of STS contain somatic genetic aberrations, including specific genetic mutations and
nonspecific genetic alterations associated with complex, unbalanced karyotypes. Molecular genetic testing has
emerged as a powerful ancillary testing approach to identify STS types and render prognostic information.
The number of genomic alterations correlates with the histologic grade and aggressiveness of sarcomas. An
ever-increasing number of somatic gene mutations have been found in STS, including those of the

P13KCA

HMGA2
genes. Unique nonrandom
chromosomal translocations have been found in many STS, including Ewing’s sarcoma, clear-cell sarcoma,
myxoid/round-cell liposarcoma, alveolar rhabdomyosarcoma, desmoplastic small round-cell tumors, synovial
sarcoma, and dermatofibrosarcoma protuberans. Abnormal somatic genetic protein products provide potential
targets for sarcoma-specific therapy.
Clinical Presentation
The most common presentation of an STS is a slowly enlarging painless mass. Although one-third of patients
are completely asymptomatic, associated presenting symptoms may include pain, compressive symptoms,
fever, and weight loss. Sarcoma tends not to invade other structures, but rather to have a pushing type of
growth along tissue planes. In addition, these tumors tend not to compress luminal structures, such as the
intestine or blood vessels. The presence of significant neurovascular or GI compressive or obstructive
symptoms implies locally advanced disease. Additional worrisome clinical features are a history of a rapid
growth and presence of lymphadenopathy. Although benign soft tissue masses are very common, a mass that
is increasing in size, measures over 5 cm, or is painful should be considered an STS until proven otherwise.
Diagnosis and Staging
Patients with suspected STS should be referred to a specialist for diagnosis and definitive treatment.
Ultrasound can be used as a screening exam to evaluate for any suspicious characteristics, such as
heterogeneity, necrosis, or margin irregularity. Plain x-ray films are useful in the initial assessment of masses
associated with bones and joints, and in evaluating for bone destruction. When a patient presents with a
clinically suspicious mass, appropriate imaging and staging studies are carried out to determine the extent of
local disease and whether there is any metastatic disease (Figure 22-13).

MRI is valuable in assessing soft tissue masses of the extremities, thorax, head, and neck, whereas CT is
utilized for the delineation of retroperitoneal and visceral sarcomas. PET and PET/CT are not recommended
for initial evaluation of patients with suspicious soft tissue masses unless an MPNST is suspected in a patient
with neurofibromatosis.
Core-needle biopsy of the suspicious mass is undertaken after discussion in a multidisciplinary setting to
ensure the biopsy is done in the correct location in a region of viable tumor. FNA is not recommended as a
primary diagnostic tool because of the lack of adequate tissue to assess tumor histology or grade. Endoscopic
or image-guided biopsy may be necessary for thoracic, abdominal, pelvic, or deep-extremity tumors. Multiple
cores are encouraged to rule out tumor heterogeneity and to ensure that detailed histologic and
immunohistochemistry studies can be performed. If core biopsy yields inadequate tissue for diagnosis, then an
open biopsy is performed in the axial plane that would be used for excision of the lesion, with minimal
dissection and careful attention to hemostasis, per NCCN guidelines. Resection with adequate margins of
normal tissue will be sufficient for the management of small (≤5 cm), superficial, well-differentiated lesions.
All other tumors require multidisciplinary management, with many of the components of treatment decided
by a team prior to definitive surgery.
STSs arise from a variety of cell types, and are, therefore, challenging to diagnose. Anatomic location and
histology are used to narrow down the list of potential tumor types. Using panels of immunohistochemical
stains, a pathologist can accurately identify the more common histologic types. For example, myogenin
identifies the immature skeletal muscle of rhabdomyosarcoma, whereas CD31 identifies the vascular
endothelium of angiosarcoma. Molecular assays can also be used to identify genetic abnormalities unique to
specific STSs. Once identified, histologic subtypes allow STS to be classified as having either limited or
significant metastatic potential. Lymph node metastases are not a common feature of sarcoma, occurring in
<5% of tumors, exceptions being histologic subtypes such as epithelioid sarcoma, rhabdomyosarcoma, clear-
cell sarcoma, and angiosarcoma. The metastatic tumor spread is hematogenous, primarily to the lung;
however, in advanced disease, subcutaneous metastases are not uncommon. For intra-and retroperitoneal
disease, liver metastases and eventual sarcomatosis (extensive sarcoma tumor nodules within the peritoneal
cavity) are common in the terminal phases of the disease.
As with other cancers, sarcoma is staged according to the AJCC staging criteria. The overall clinical
behavior of most sarcomas is similar and is determined by anatomic location, grade, and the size of tumor.
Smaller lesions (≤5 cm T1 lesions) tend to have a better prognosis. Tumor grade (Table 22-4) also provides
important prognostic information, with higher-grade lesions more likely to spread or recur. Prior to any
definitive surgical procedures, a metastatic workup is performed. Chest CT is recommended for the
assessment of pulmonary metastatic disease. CT of the abdomen and pelvis are also recommended in patients
with round-cell or myxoid liposarcomas because of their propensity to metastasize to the abdomen and
retroperitoneum.

Treatment
STSs are predominantly treated with surgery. The surgical goals include local control while maximizing
function and limiting morbidity. Therapy is individualized; however, the surgeon strives for total en bloc
removal without traversing the tumor, obtaining adequate margins (at least 1 cm) of normal tissue completely
surrounding the tumor. Surgical therapy alone may be all that is required for the successful management of
small (<5 cm), low-grade, superficial (to fascia) tumors. Larger and/or high-grade STS warrant adjuvant (in
addition to, but after, surgery) radiation therapy. In addition, when the ability to obtain a 1-cm margin is in
doubt owing to the close proximity of vital structures such as major nerves or arteries, adjuvant or neoadjuvant
(in addition to, but before, surgery) radiotherapy, or chemoradiotherapy is employed. This strategy improves
not only the limb-sparing rate (fewer amputations) but also local control. Administering neoadjuvant
radiotherapy for retroperitoneal tumors can be problematic, given the limited tissue tolerances of certain
organs (e.g., liver, 2,000 rads). When margins are positive or very close (<2 mm), the local recurrence rate
approaches 100%. Although systemic adjuvant chemotherapy is commonly utilized in children with STS, its
use in adults is on an individualized basis, carefully balancing the potential benefit with anticipated toxicities.

Retroperitoneal Sarcoma
Figure 22-16 demonstrates a large heterogeneous right retroperitoneal liposarcoma, which has pushed the
right kidney out from the retroperitoneal space. Two components of the tumor are visible: the darker, lateral
area more consistent with simple fat and a more solid central component compressing the aorta.
Retroperitoneal STSs are typically asymptomatic until they reach a large size and compress or invade
surrounding structures. The differential diagnosis includes lymphoma and metastatic germ cell tumors. A
thoracoabdominal incision was necessary to completely excise this tumor. En bloc resection required resecting
the tumor, right kidney, adrenal gland, and right colon. Complete surgical excision with negative (R0)
margins is, in most cases, the only curative treatment. Unfortunately, the ability to achieve a wide resection
margin within the peritoneum or retroperitoneum is almost impossible owing to adjacent vital structures, and
local recurrences are common. Neoadjuvant radiation therapy may be recommended for large, high-grade, or
initially unresectable tumors. Intraoperative radiation therapy can also be considered if a close margin is
anticipated. Adjuvant RT is considered, although not routinely, for intermediate/high-grade histology or
positive resection margins, within the tolerance of surrounding structures. Adjuvant chemotherapy is generally
not administered outside of a clinical trial.

Management of Local Recurrence
Even in the presence of local recurrence, STS remains primarily a surgical disease. Typically, sarcomas recur
within 2 years of the original presentation. Confirmation of the diagnosis of local recurrence is done by
image-guided core biopsy. Imaging studies (CT and/or MRI) are required to delineate the extent of local
recurrence and determine further resectability. Additional imaging studies are carried out (chest CT) to
restage the patient for metastatic disease. Excision of local recurrence is always attempted; however, obtaining
clear margins may not be feasible. In extremity STS, extensive involvement of vital structures may warrant
amputation. If the recurrence is isolated and can be managed with resection and there is no associated
metastatic disease, long-term prognosis may not be impacted. However, the outcome of patients who develop
local recurrence is poorer than that of those who do not, and further local recurrence and subsequent
development of metastatic disease is heavily dependent on the adequacy of the original surgery, grade of the
original tumor, and subsequent recurrences. Dedifferentiation from low to high grade is uncommon but may
occur in liposarcoma. If not previously administered, radiotherapy may be of value in controlling further local
recurrence or making unresectable local recurrence resectable. Alternate delivery of RT, such as brachytherapy
or intensity-modulated RT, can be considered in the previously radiated patient.
Management of Distant Disease
The majority of patients who develop distant metastatic STS are incurable; however, opportunities for cure
should not be overlooked. Per NCCN guidelines, isolated metastases can be treated with metastasectomy with
or without preoperative or postoperative chemotherapy and with or without RT. Other management options
are ablation, embolization, or stereotactic body radiation therapy. Resection of isolated pulmonary metastases
can result in survival rates of up to 40%. Additional palliative options in the face of more widely disseminated
disease include observation and supportive care. Palliative chemotherapy, usually doxorubicin-based
combination chemotherapy, is administered to improve quality of life and prolong survival. Response rates to
chemotherapy are poor and the median survival after developing distant metastases is 12 to 19 months.
However, survival is dependent upon tumor biology and despite unresectable disease, some patients survive 2
to 3 years. Enrollment in clinical trials testing new strategies should be encouraged. Novel therapies are being
developed, including next-generation sequencing, to identify candidates for molecularly targeted therapies.
Prognosis
Overall, patient 5-year survival rate ranges from 90% for superficial low-grade tumors to 20% for advanced
(metastatic, or large, deep, or high-grade local) disease. In addition, resection margin involvement is an
unfavorable survival factor (Table 22-5). Blood tests are not of value in the follow-up of STS. For patients
with superficial low-grade stage I STS excised for cure, clinical examination every 6 months (for the first 2 to
3 years), then yearly, is adequate follow-up. Chest imaging using x-ray or CT every 6 to 12 months can be
considered. For deep-extremity or retroperitoneal stage II/III STS, imaging with CT or MRI will detect local
recurrence. A baseline postoperative imaging study is helpful for later comparison. Because these tumors have
a higher risk of metastasizing, chest x-ray or chest CT is recommended, beginning every 3 to 6 months for 2
to 3 years, then every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.

Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor
GIST represents a subgroup of sarcoma arising from the cell of Cajal in the myenteric plexus in the
muscularis mucosa of GI neural origin (Figure 22-18). Tumors most commonly occur in the stomach and
proximal small intestine; however, they also develop in the more distal GI tract, omentum, mesentery, and
peritoneum. They may be asymptomatic or present with GI bleeding or abdominal pain. GISTs occur
primarily in middle-age and older individuals, and approximately 5% are part of inherited familial syndromes.
CT with IV/oral contrast is utilized to characterize the tumor, which has a smooth border and enhances
brightly with IV contrast. These tumors are unique in that they have a specific genetic makeup and may
express CD34 (hematopoietic progenitor cell antigen) and CD117 (C-kit protein, a membrane receptor with
a tyrosine kinase component) antigens. GIST is characterized by the presence of somatic mutation of c-kit
(80% to 85%) or platelet-derived growth factor receptor-A (PDFGR-A) gene (10%), whereas 5% to 10%
harbor none of these gene mutations. Unlike other STSs, GIST uncommonly metastasizes to the lungs but
almost always recurs in the liver and/or peritoneal surface. Tumor size, mitotic rate, and location correlate
with the rate of progression-free survival. Histologic tumor grade is determined by mitotic rate. Surgical
resection should strive for negative margins, and regional lymphadenectomy is usually not indicated. In the
past, this tumor had a poor prognosis; however, the recent development of targeted chemotherapy in the form
of tyrosine kinase inhibitors targeting c-kit and PDGFRA, such as imatinib mesylate, has shown impressive
results in reversing and stabilizing metastatic disease. In the metastatic setting, 3 to 9 months of imatinib
therapy followed by hepatic metastasectomy can provide prolonged progression-free survival. Postoperatively,
long-term tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy is generally recommended.

gene. They have also
been associated with high estrogen states, such as pregnancy. Primary observation is acceptable for
asymptomatic tumors. Surgical treatment consists of a wide resection with negative microscopic margins, if
feasible. When this is not possible, radiotherapy is a reasonable primary therapeutic option. More recently,
evidence has emerged that some tumors may respond to nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, tamoxifen, or
some combination of these agents. Response to these agents is typically slow but can continue for months or
years. For recurrent lesions, a combination of surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy is used. Tyrosine kinase
inhibitors, such as imatinib, are effective for unresectable, recurrent, and/or metastatic desmoid tumors. In
cases of extensive local disease, imatinib can be used neoadjuvantly, which can render the tumor resectable
after months of therapy. Cytotoxic chemotherapy can also be utilized for tumors that are advanced, are
unresectable, or have failed prior therapy.

Kaposi’s Sarcoma
Kaposi’s sarcoma (KS) is a low-grade malignancy that in the past was largely limited to elderly Jewish men of
Mediterranean descent and to people from sub-Saharan Africa. With the AIDS epidemic, the incidence of
KS has increased. There are now four subtypes of KS based on epidemiologic variations: classic KS; African
endemic KS; iatrogenic (immunosuppression-related) KS; and epidemic, AIDS-associated KS. KS is the most
common neoplastic complication of AIDS and is considered an AIDS-defining illness. Homosexual and
bisexual men are much more likely to have KS than others with AIDS. This finding suggests a sexually
transmitted etiology in this patient population, and the causative agent appears to be human herpesvirus 8
(HHV8). Iatrogenic KS can occur in patients immunosuppressed by drug therapy and may regress if the
immunotherapy is halted.
KS lesions initially appear as asymptomatic, flat, blue patches that resemble a hematoma. Later, they
become raised, rubbery nodules. Non-AIDS KS is typically indolent, cutaneous, and found on the lower
extremities. AIDS-related KS often begins in the perioral mucosa, most commonly, in the palate. AIDS-
related KS is often multifocal, with rapid spread to the lymph nodes and associated lymphedema. It often
involves the GI tract, presenting as GI bleeding, obstruction, and dysphagia. Other areas that can be involved
include the respiratory organs, liver, spleen, and bone marrow. Biopsy demonstrates an angiosarcoma with
fibroblasts, spindle cells, and increased capillary growth. Risk assessment of AIDS-related KS is based on
tumor location, immune status including CD4 counts, and associated systemic illness/performance status.
Classic KS lesions that are localized and symptomatic can be managed by excision or curettage. In AIDS-
related KS, potent combination antiretroviral therapy (ART) is effective and may be the only therapy required
for symptom palliation. A small percentage of patients may develop progression of KS with the initiation of
ART. Discontinuation of systemic steroids can also facilitate regression. Local treatment options for
symptomatic sites include intralesional chemotherapy, usually vinblastine, or radiation therapy for larger areas.
Systemic chemotherapy is reserved for advanced symptomatic or rapidly progressive KS. Pegylated liposomal
doxorubicin is the first-line agent, with response rates of 30% to 60%. The tolerability of liposomal
doxorubicin can be poor in this population due to their poor performance status, concurrent opportunistic
infections, and toxicities from ART. Responses to liposomal doxorubicin can be observed rapidly and
dramatically after a few treatments. Recent literature suggests that once the CD4 count is 400 or above and
most of the lesions either regress or are asymptomatic, liposomal doxorubicin can be stopped. Further
regression occurs, which is likely due to reconstitution of the immune system. Paclitaxel is used as a second-
line or alternate systemic therapy, taking care to minimize steroid premedications.

Answers and Explanations
1. Answer: C
The patient presented in this question has a mole that fulfills several criteria (i.e. A, Asymmetry; B,
Borders; C, Color; D, Diameter; E, Evolution) to be sufficiently suspicious for melanoma to merit
biopsy. There are multiple methods for biopsy of skin lesions and each has its own limitations. The most
appropriate next step in the diagnosis of a suspicious mole is excisional biopsy with removal of the entire
lesion with a 1-to 2-mm margin of normal skin. Repeat skin examination in 1 year is not consistent with
the need for immediate biopsy. Superficial shave biopsy is not the most appropriate method of biopsy of
a skin lesion that is suspicious for melanoma because it fails to provide accurate information related to the
depth of invasion should the lesion prove to be a melanoma. Microscopic tumor depth of invasion in the
skin is an important prognostic factor in the staging of melanoma. Needle biopsy would not be an
appropriate method of biopsy of a mole because it does not yield sufficient tissue for the pathologist to
determine if the mole is a melanoma. Pathologists prefer removal of the entire lesion so they can examine
it in its entirety. Moh’s micrographic surgery is a specialized surgical technique to precisely remove a skin
cancer with clear margins while healthy tissue is spared. Moh’s surgery is relatively expensive but may be
indicated in anatomically important areas (eyelid, nose, lips) where sparing normal tissue and local
control are important. Moh’s is not appropriate in the patient presented in the question because no
diagnosis has been made yet, and the preservation of normal tissue is not as important on the forearm as
it might be on the face. For more information on this topic, please see the section on Diagnosis under
the heading Melanoma.
2. Answer: D
Once a diagnosis of melanoma is made, the next steps in treatment involve (1) addressing the local
disease to reduce the risk of local recurrence and (2) determining which patients are at risk for tumor
spread to the regional lymph nodes. In the absence of any known metastatic disease, both steps are
predicated on an accurate depth of invasion of the primary melanoma. Wide excision is indicated
following biopsy, even if the margins of the original excision are free of tumor, to ensure removal of
tumor cells outside the borders of the lesion. In addition to addressing the local tumor, the next step in
staging involves determining the status of the regional nodes by SLN biopsy. Follow-up alone would not
be appropriate in a patient with a melanoma 1.5 mm in depth. PET/CT is used for staging, but the yield
is not high enough to justify its use unless the tumor is >4 mm in depth or the patient has known
metastatic disease. As noted in the explanation for the correct answer, wide excision alone is inadequate.
Moh’s surgery is not indicated for a back melanoma because preservation of normal tissue is not as
important as it might be on the face. For more information on this topic, please see the section on
Treatment under the heading Melanoma.
3. Answer: A
The presence of a 3-cm firm groin mass in a 65-year-old woman requires a thorough evaluation. She has
already undergone an FNA of the mass demonstrating atypical lymphocytes; therefore, the next most
appropriate step is complete removal—an excisional biopsy—of the mass for pathologic examination
(lymphoma is suspected). Bone marrow aspiration may be indicated after a diagnosis of lymphoma. CT
scan of the abdomen and pelvis and medical oncology referral are not indicated at this point until a
definitive tissue diagnosis is obtained. Repeat FNA is unlikely to yield any additional information, given
the first FNA result showing atypical lymphocytes. For more information on this topic, please see the
section on Diagnosis and Staging under the heading Sarcoma.
4. Answer: D
STSs arise from the mesenchymal tissue, and the most common sites in adults are the extremities. The
most common presentation is a mass that is increasing in size, and delays in diagnosis are common.
Adequate tissue can be obtained by core biopsy. This procedure is best performed using image guidance
and it can be done under local anesthesia. Excisional biopsy of STSs disturbs tissue planes and may
produce hematomas that compromise definitive resections and may even lead to amputation. FNA
biopsy will not yield enough tissue to make an accurate diagnosis and to determine the histologic type
and tumor grade. Bone scan would not be appropriate prior to a tissue diagnosis. In the absence of a
family history suggestive of Li-Fraumeni syndrome, genetic testing is not indicated. For more
information on this topic, please see the section on Diagnosis and Staging under the heading Sarcoma.
5. Answer: B
Unlike other STSs, GIST tumors uncommonly metastasize to the lungs but more frequently spread to
the liver and/or peritoneal surfaces. GIST tumors are frequently associated with a mutation in the c-kit
gene, which encodes for the expression of CD117 (c-kit protein, a membrane receptor with a tyrosine
kinase component) antigen. Recently, imatinib (Gleevec), a tyrosine kinase inhibitor targeting c-kit, has
been found to be effective in treating metastatic GIST tumors. People who inherit only one copy of the
tumor suppressor gene, p53, have Li-Fraumeni syndrome, which is associated with several tumors,
including breast cancer, brain tumors, adrenal cortical carcinoma, acute leukemia, and bone and STSs.
Amplification of the Her2-neu oncogene gene or overexpression of its protein product is associated with
poor prognosis in breast cancer. CEA is an oncofetal antigen associated with colorectal and other
cancers, whereas N-myc is an oncogene that is amplified in neuroblastoma. For more information on this
topic, please see the section on Gastrointestinal Stromal Tumor.

PERIOPERATIVE MANAGEMENT OF THE PEDIATRIC SURGICAL PATIENT
Fluids and Electrolytes
Fluid and electrolyte management in pediatric patients must be extremely precise, given the narrow margin
between dehydration and fluid overload. Compared with adults, infants and children have greater metabolic
demands, and because they turn over body water and electrolytes so rapidly, pediatric patients may undergo
rapid, major shifts in body fluid compartments. The immature neonatal kidney has limited concentrating and
diluting capacities and therefore cannot be entirely relied upon to compensate for a deficiency or
overabundance of fluids and electrolytes. Although a child’s need may be estimated according to standard
formulas, there is no substitute for frequent adjustments based on careful monitoring of the patient.
Neonates have a significantly greater proportion of total body water than adults because newborns have a
larger pool of extracellular fluid (ECF) (Figure 23-1). This fluid compartment is increased further in
extremely premature infants (<28 weeks’ gestation). At birth, the ECF is even more expanded, and as much as
10% of birth weight is lost during the first week as this surplus water is excreted.

Maintenance Requirements
Maintenance fluids and electrolytes are the quantities that must be provided to compensate for normal renal
excretion and insensible losses through the skin and lungs. Table 23-1 provides guidelines for calculating the
amounts of water and electrolytes required. In addition, a minimal quantity of glucose is included to provide
for some protein sparing and to avoid hypoglycemia. These constituents can all be provided by 5% dextrose
(D5%) in ½ normal saline + 20 mEq/L KCl in infants and D5% in normal saline + 20 mEq/L KCl in older
children at the infusion rate calculated in Table 23-1. The patient’s electrolytes should be monitored closely
when there is an extended period of nil per os (NPO) and when there are significant gastrointestinal (GI)
fluid losses as in the instance of a bowel obstruction.

Preexisting Deficits
Children with acute surgical illness may have significant fluid and electrolyte deficits from poor oral intake,
vomiting, diarrhea, peritonitis, sepsis, burns, or hemorrhage. Intravascular volume must be rapidly restored to
maintain adequate tissue perfusion for normal organ function. Most surgical diseases cause isotonic
dehydration. Fluid deficits are best corrected empirically in stages, as outlined in Table 23-2.
